title: The cilantro "soap" gene
hook: To some people, fresh coriander leaves taste exactly like a bar of soap.
peek: Fresh coriander, or cilantro, is a beloved herb for most people and tastes like soap to a minority. Part of the reason seems to be in their genes, in a smell receptor tuned to the same molecules used in soap.
lede: Fresh coriander leaves, called cilantro in North America, are central to cooking from Mexico to Thailand. Yet a minority of people say the herb tastes like soap. They are not being fussy. The leaves contain aldehydes, a family of molecules that also show up in soaps and lotions, and some noses seem especially tuned to them.

bullets.text: Researchers working with the genetics company 23andMe compared tens of thousands of customers and found a variant linked to the soapy taste, near a cluster of smell receptor genes that includes OR6A2, which responds to aldehydes.

Identical twins agree about coriander more often than non-identical twins, another hint of a genetic part. The one gene variant found so far explains only a small share, though, and familiarity matters a lot.

Much of what we call taste is really smell, picked up by hundreds of different receptor types. Small differences in those receptors can make the same food smell different to two people at the same table.
The cookery writer Julia Child said in interviews that she disliked the herb and would pick it out of her food. She is often held up as the most famous member of the soap camp.
Like the famous dress that looked blue to some and white to others, the herb is a reminder that perception is personal, built from the same input but processed in different ways.
The food writer Harold McGee has suggested that crushing the leaves lets enzymes break down some of the aldehydes, so a pounded sauce may taste milder to people who find the fresh leaves soapy.
